ch00.note: So popular was The Whistling Wind on its serialization in 1943 that publishers dubbed the year 徐觑年, ‘the Year of Xu Xu’—a description borne out by scholarship on the period. This ‘About the Author’ page is the source edition’s own front matter, not written by Xu Xu.

ch00.anchor: Yu Lihua, Ji Zheng and Nie Hualing
ch00.note: Three writers of the postwar Chinese diaspora. Yu Lihua (於梨華, 1929–2020) and Nie Hualing (聚華艮, 1925–2024, co-founder of the Iowa International Writing Program) are well documented; Ji Zheng (吉鈕) was a Taiwanese novelist of the same ‘overseas-student’ school, more thinly recorded.

ch01.note: C. L. Stephen, an American naval medical officer and soon the narrator’s closest friend, whose acquaintance the following chapters recount. The name 史蒂芬 transliterates the English ‘Stephen.’

ch02.anchor: the foreign concessions still kept their peculiar standing
ch02.note: After Japan occupied the Chinese-administered districts of Shanghai in 1937, the foreign concessions—the International Settlement and the French Concession—stayed under British, American, French and other control, policed by their own garrisons, until Japan seized them after Pearl Harbor in December 1941. This anomalous enclave was known as the Solitary Island (see Chapter 3).

ch03.note: 孤岛 (gudao), the name for the foreign concessions of Shanghai in 1937–41, when they survived as islands of neutral territory ringed by Japanese-held China. Also Englished as the ‘isolated’ or ‘orphan’ island.
Bai Ping (白芨), a dancer at the Paramount and one of the three women at the novel’s centre; she is introduced in the next chapter.

ch04.note: William Hazlitt’s Table-Talk (two volumes, 1821–22) is a real collection of familiar essays; the piece the narrator recalls is most likely ‘On Living to One’s-Self,’ Hazlitt’s meditation on a life led apart from the world.

ch04.anchor: A camellia that belongs to any man
ch04.note: The exchange sets a rose (which belongs to no one) against a camellia (which belongs to any man). In its literary code the camellia is the flower of the courtesan—as in Dumas’s La Dame aux camélias (茶花女)—and Bai Ping applies it to herself, a dance-hostess.
St Ignatius Cathedral at Xujiahui (older spelling Zikawei), in southwest Shanghai: a Gothic church built by French Jesuits in 1906–10 and the seat of Shanghai Catholicism.

ch05.anchor: a heart as solemn and translucent as this
ch05.note: The source text of this clause is garbled—愿我用就有这样庄严与透明的心灵, in which 用就 appears to be a corruption of 永/永远 (‘always’). The sense ‘may I too always have a heart as solemn and translucent as this’ is rendered here; the defect is left visible rather than silently smoothed over.

ch06.note: A pun: 红心 is at once the winning red of the roulette table where they had gambled, the ‘hearts’ of a card suit, and a ‘red heart’ in the sense of sincerity—so that her stake was laid on his affections.

ch07.note: In Greek myth Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection and pined away into the flower that bears his name. The source uses an older, now-superseded transliteration, 纳虚仙子 (modern 纳西索斯).
Claude Debussy (1862–1918), French composer, a central figure of musical Impressionism.
Helen, a shy, music-loving young American, the third of the novel’s principal women. Her surname, 曼斯儿, transliterates a Western name the source does not spell out; ‘Manfield’ is a reconstruction.

ch08.note: The orchestra of the Shanghai Municipal Council (工部局), long conducted by Mario Paci and reckoned the finest in the Far East; it gave the Chinese premiere of Beethoven’s Ninth in 1936, and a 1939 performance paired it with a large local chorus. The narrator’s explanation that the concert was moved to the evening because the chorus could not all be free by day is his own detail, not independently corroborated.
Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854), German Idealist philosopher, a contemporary of Fichte and Hegel—fitting reading for a narrator at work on a book about ethics and aesthetics.
